extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in simple living, self-reliance, and practical philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Advice-driven personal essay arguing for simple, economical, and self-reliant living: how to reduce possessions and labour, grow and prepare one's own food, and approach charity and cooperation. Uses concrete household detail and personal accounting as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live simply and work minimally
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain oneself largely by simple manual labor so that most of the year is free for study and thought; work only as much as necessary to secure independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Thoreau's claim that by "working about six weeks in a year, I could meet all the expenses of living" and that sustaining oneself can be "not a hardship but a pastime, if we will live simply and wisely." Use concrete accounting and examples of limited labor to justify the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize and lighten possessions (avoid 'trumpery')
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep furniture and belongings to the bare essentials; view accumulated household goods as encumbrances that reduce mobility and freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by vivid imagery of people moving with overloaded furniture and the injunction that "if I have got to drag my trap, I will take care that it be a light one." Use lists of minimal furniture (bed, table, desk, three chairs, etc.) and contrast with auctioned 'trumpery' to show the cost of excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make and source your own food where practical
rubrics_metrics.description: Raise or prepare your own staples (rye, Indian meal), make substitutes (molasses from pumpkins or beets), and rely on simple diets to reduce dependence on markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed descriptions of bread-making (hoe-cakes, mixture of rye and Indian meal), preserving loaves, and producing molasses are offered as practical evidence. Include concrete costs and experiments (what succeeded and failed) to make the case credible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use transparent household accounting to justify lifestyle
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep and publish detailed accounts of expenses and earnings to demonstrate that a simple life is economically feasible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoreau lists itemized food, clothing, and household costs and a balance of earnings vs. outgoes. Present such statistics verbatim or in similar detail to lend authority and counter objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer self-sufficiency over market dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible, avoid buying processed staples from distant markets; instead cultivate, grind, and prepare basic foods locally to increase independence and reduce cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: "Every New Englander might easily raise all his own breadstuffs...and grind them in a hand-mill." Argue from local agronomy and small-scale techniques rather than from industrial supply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose occupations that preserve freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor kinds of labor that require limited time or allow immediate start (day-labor, short seasonal work) rather than professions that absorb one's entire life and identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoreau praises day-labor because "the laborer’s day ends with the going down of the sun" and it may require only thirty or forty days a year to support one. Use comparisons with teaching, trade, and long careers to show trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find and follow your own way
rubrics_metrics.description: Each person should discover and pursue his or her own vocation or mode of life, rather than inherit or imitate parents' or neighbors' ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expressed as: "I would have each one be very careful to find out and pursue his own way." Encourage experimentation and emphasize individuality as a moral and practical principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be skeptical about coöperation and communal arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that most forms of cooperation are partial or superficial; coöperation often imposes constraints (waiting for others, thin common walls) and may not be worth the compromise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the travel anecdote (two men traveling together, one with money) and discussion of shared walls to illustrate how dependence on others can hinder immediate action and freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice a periodic purification of possessions and life ('busk')
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt ritualized purging of worn-out goods and a renewal (like the described 'busk') to prevent accumulation and to symbolically recommit to simplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite the Mucclasse Indian custom and Mexican purification every fifty-two years as models. Recommend a regular clearing-out and symbolic re-firing to renew the household and community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique and temper philanthropy—do good that actually helps
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware philanthropy that is self-regarding, theatrical, or that perpetuates dependency; aim for aid that addresses real needs and does not spread ‘disease’ or despair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoreau warns that philanthropy is often "tainted" and "greatly overrated," and that one should 'give the poor the aid they most need' and 'spend yourself with it.' Emphasize concrete, effective help over display, and consider unintended consequences of charitable acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid charity that treats symptoms instead of roots
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not waste resources on measures that only scratch at effects; prioritize actions and modes of life that address root causes of poverty and misery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: giving a tenth of income versus spending the nine tenths to change conditions; the idea that many efforts are 'hacking at the branches' rather than striking at the root. Encourage strategic, systemic thinking and self-reflection on how one's own lifestyle contributes to social problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct your own condition before attempting widespread reform
rubrics_metrics.description: A reformer must attend to his or her own health and inner life before trying to restore or reform others; personal well-being makes philanthropic or reform work effective rather than bitter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoreau: 'what so saddens the reformer is...his private ail. Let this be righted'—use this as guidance to stress self-care and authenticity before public moralizing.
